slides.title: Python Basics
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter is the prompt, the values it computes with, the operators that combine them, the names that remember them, and a first program. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and what the run printed as a table, chart or drawing.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Four parts: values and types, operations, names and functions, and a first program. Each range is a run of slides you can jump to. The chapter-code tab of the page holds the same examples in the same order.

slides.title: Three questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Three questions to carry through the chapter. Which operations can raise an error, and which? Which results can surprise a student? And what has changed in current Python since the book?

slides.title: Part 1: Values and types
slides.say: Part one. The shell evaluates an expression and prints its value. Every value has a data type: integer, float or string. Notice which results surprise you.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: values and types
slides.say: A calculator with a screen is the shell. An expression is a recipe line that ends in one value. A data type is the label on a container. Ask students to add their own everyday picture.

slides.title: The shell: type an expression, get a value
slides.say: The shell is a calculator that answers. In a program you write print yourself. Ask students to predict 2 + 3 * 6 before the run, and why it is not 30.

slides.title: Story: a Christmas hobby named after a comedy troupe
slides.say: Guido van Rossum began Python in the Christmas week of 1989 at CWI in Amsterdam. The name comes from Monty Python. Ask students which of today's examples they would have written in a language without this readability.

slides.title: Data types: int, float and str
slides.say: Type names the data type of any value. A whole number plus a float gives a float. Ask: what type does 7 + 1.0 have, and why?

slides.title: Integers never overflow
slides.say: Python integers never overflow. 2 to the power 100 has 31 digits and is exact. Int turns text into a number, and cuts a float without rounding.

slides.title: Floats are honest about being approximate
slides.say: Zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three. Floats are binary fractions, so many decimals do not fit. Division with a slash always gives a float.

slides.title: Strings: text between quotes
slides.say: A string is text between quotes. Len counts characters. The text seven and the number seven are different values; Python never converts between them silently.

slides.title: Part 2: Operations
slides.say: Part two. Operators combine values. Precedence decides who goes first, and parentheses override it. Plus and star also work on strings, with a different meaning.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: operators
slides.say: Operators are verbs between values. Precedence is the order of work: chop before you stir. Go through the eight pictures and ask which one students remember best.

slides.title: Seven operators for numbers
slides.say: Seven operators: plus, minus, times, divide, floor divide, remainder, power. The slash always gives a float. The double slash and the percent sign work as a pair.

slides.title: Who goes first: operator precedence
slides.say: The power goes first, then times and divide, then plus and minus. Parentheses override. Minus three to the power two is minus nine, because the power binds tighter. Predict, then run.

slides.title: Division three ways: quotient and remainder
slides.say: Twenty-three candies in boxes of seven: three boxes and two left. Floor division gives the boxes, percent gives the rest. Floor division rounds down, so minus seven by two is minus four.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: operations on text
slides.say: Concatenation glues strips of text, replication photocopies them. Str is the label maker that turns any value into text. Keep the pictures; the code comes next.

slides.title: String concatenation: + joins text
slides.say: Plus joins strings and adds no space. Joining text to a number is a TypeError, because Python does not convert silently. Str fixes it. Errors are answers: read the message.

slides.title: String replication: * repeats text
slides.say: Star repeats a string. The count must be a whole number; a float raises a TypeError. Zero copies give the empty string. The chart shows how long each result is.

slides.title: Part 3: Names and functions
slides.say: Part three. A variable is a name for a value. Print shows, input reads, and str, int, float and len convert and measure. Errors are answers too.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: names
slides.say: A variable is a labelled jar. Print is the loudspeaker, input is the suggestion box. Everything in the box is paper, so even a number arrives as text.

slides.title: Variables: names that remember
slides.say: An assignment gives a name to a value. Assign again and the name refers to a new value. Names are case-sensitive: Spam was never assigned, so Python raises a NameError.

slides.title: print: the function that shows
slides.say: Print takes any number of items. The options sep and end change the separator and the ending. Print with nothing in the parentheses writes an empty line.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: functions and modules
slides.say: Len is a ruler for text. Int and float are machines with a slot in and a slot out. Ask which machine rejects the input and why.

slides.title: Conversions and len: built-in functions
slides.say: Str, int and float convert. Len counts characters; a number has no length, so convert it to text first. The table shows input, function, result and type.

slides.title: Errors are answers too
slides.say: A ValueError means the type is right but the content is wrong. A TypeError means the type itself does not fit the operation. Reading the error name tells you where to look.

slides.title: input always returns text
slides.say: Input always returns text, even when the person types a number. Plus on text glues, plus on numbers adds. Convert with int before you calculate.

slides.title: Modules: import opens a toolbox
slides.say: Import brings in a toolbox. The dot reaches inside it for a function, sqrt, or a value, pi. Standard library modules are free and always installed.

slides.title: Part 4: A first program
slides.say: Part four. A first program uses everything so far. Then we take it apart line by line, and finish with the binary digits behind every number.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: a program and its bits
slides.say: A program is a recipe. Dissecting it is taking a clock apart. Binary is a row of light switches. Each picture comes back on the slide that follows.

slides.title: Story: where hello, world began, in 1972
slides.say: The first hello, world was in a 1972 tutorial for the language B. In B the text needed three variables; in Python it is one line. Ask what a first program proves: that writing, running and seeing output all work.

slides.title: Your first program
slides.say: The first program greets, asks, measures and calculates. Because the page has no keyboard, the example names the text input would return. Trace it line by line in the table.

slides.title: Dissecting the program: join or fill in
slides.say: Two ways to build the same sentence: join five pieces with plus and str, or fill slots in an f-string. The f-string is shorter and needs no str. Which would you rather read?

slides.title: Story: Leibniz wrote every number with only 0 and 1
slides.say: Leibniz described binary arithmetic in 1679 and in a paper for the Paris Academy in 1703. Bouvet's letter from Peking showed the I Ching hexagrams as binary numbers. Ask: why do computers prefer two digits?

slides.title: How computers store numbers: binary
slides.say: Bin shows binary digits, int with base 2 reads them. Eight binary digits make a byte and hold 256 values. Each place is a power of two; the chart shows which places are on for the number five.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. The shell and its error messages improved in 3.13. The free-threaded build is experimental. F-strings have a formal grammar. Check each row against its source.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples of each part. Everything is on the chapter page, in the same order.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter and the Python tutorial. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and one video and read or watch it before the next class.
